newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain Civil War veterans caught up in new battle.
newsitem.headline: Spain Civil War veterans caught up in new battle.

text.p: Foreign veterans visiting Madrid to help commemorate the outbreak of the Spanish Civil War 60 years ago found themselves caught in a crossfire of words on Thursday.

Critics of Spain's conservative government accused it of failing to send any senior representatives to a ceremony in parliament at which the veterans were granted the right to opt for Spanish citizenship.

Nearly 400 one-time members of the International Brigades arrived in Spain this week to recall their taking up of arms to fight for the Republican cause in a conflict which became an ideological rehearsal for World War Two.
Despite the passing years, their presence was once more controversial with left-wing politicians accusing the ruling Popular Party (PP) of snubbing them out of political spite.
"It was a sorry sight the right wing offered in the Spanish parliament yesterday," said the daily newspaper Diario 16."It is not a question of ideology but of style, manners and culture."

Officials said neither Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar nor King Juan Carlos were scheduled to take part in events for the foreigners who fought General Francisco Franco's troops after he revolted against the Republican government in July 1936.
According to another daily, El Pais, Aznar had previously told one veteran in a letter that he would receive them with pleasure.

The Brigades were mainly recruited by communist parties and trade unions in Europe and North America, with support from the Soviet Union. The armies of Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy aided the right-wing or Nationalist side.
Republican defeat in 1939 left Franco to rule Spain as a military dictator until his death in 1975.
But the veterans found that the ghosts of the Civil War are alive and well, six months after Spaniards voted in their first right-wing government since the return of democracy.

Socialist spokesman Jesus Caldera said it was deplorable that both parliamentary speaker Federico Trillo and his deputy, Fernando Alvarez de Miranda, flouted parliament etiquette by staying away from Wednesday's ceremony.
The snub proved some members of the Spanish right were still focused on revenge, he added.
"There has been no gesture of gratitude deserved by those who, abandoning families and property, embarked in the fight for justice, dignity and freedom," Caldera told reporters.
Members of the Communist-led United Left coalition and the media joined in the chorus of disapproval.

"During this entire week the veterans will receive the tribute of people who want to transmit the gratitude of millions of Spaniards," said El Pais. "But they will also have to drink in the bitterness of those who haven't forgotten the past."
Some veterans lamented the lack of official recognition but many said the warm-hearted reaction of ordinary people and the joy of reuniting with old comrades more than made up for it.

People lined the streets and broke into spontaneous applause as veterans, many of them aged 80 and over and in wheelchairs, made their way to Madrid's sports stadium on Tuesday night for a huge party at which young and old wept with emotion.
The former brigaders also chose to smooth over a conflict surrounding the Spanish parliament's unanimous decision a year ago to grant them honourary citizenship.
The gesture fell flat when they discovered that under Spanish law it would mean renouncing their own citizenship and all the health and pension benefits available to them at home.
German veteran Julius Goldstein summed up the spirit of truce when he told parliament on Wednesday: "From now we not only carry Spain in our hearts, from today we are all Spaniards."
